data.body:
Read **Break, Move, Settle — Changing Land** with a partner or use read-aloud. Explore **Key Words**, then play Matching and Memory. Use **Keep the Ideas Clear** as a reference. Try **Sort and Explain**, **Explain Your Thinking**, and **Check Your Understanding**. Use **Remember the Ideas** to build a memory cue. Read **Questions to Explore**, then complete **Try It with Evidence**.

Explain an answer using a detail from the lesson. Pictures support the activity text. These are illustrative examples, not measured experimental results.

Picture panels: Three land processes; Ways material moves; Plan and repeat a test; Evidence and model limits. Grains and cracks may be enlarged for visibility. Arrows and streaks are drawing cues. Use real observations and measurements to test a claim.

history.title: Break, Move, Settle — Changing Land
history.data:
## Break, Move, Settle

After rain, a muddy stream crosses a path. Farther downhill, a fan of sand lies where the water spread out. Both places hold clues about how land changes.

**Weathering** breaks rock down or changes it where it is. Water can enter a crack. If that water freezes, it can push against the sides. Repeated freezing and thawing can help widen some cracks. Roots growing in cracks can also push on rock. Not every crack forms in the same way.

**Erosion** moves rock or soil from one place to another. Flowing water can carry loose grains. Wind can move dry sand. Moving ice can carry rock. Gravity can pull loose material downhill. Breaking and moving can happen together, but they name different processes.

The loose pieces are called **sediment**. Some are tiny; others are large. **Deposition** happens when moving sediment settles or is left behind. A stream that slows may drop some of its load. Different sizes can settle at different places.

A **slope** is a slant in the land. Steeper slopes can change how water moves, but slope is not the only factor. The amount of water, the soil, and plant cover also matter. **Runoff** is water moving over the land surface.

How can we test one idea? Build two small trays with the same amount and kind of soil. Set different slopes. Add equal water amounts at the same rate and place. Catch the runoff in cups. Repeat the test with fresh setups. Decide how you will measure moved soil before you start.

Your **evidence** is what you observed or measured. A darker cup may suggest more suspended soil, but color alone is not an exact mass. A **model** helps us study a process at a small scale. A tray cannot copy a whole hillside.

Use careful language in your claim. Say what happened in your test, not what must happen on every hill. A useful explanation connects the evidence to a process and names a limit of the model.

questions.question: Which example is weathering?
options: A root widening a rock crack
Mud settling in a quiet pool
questions.correctAnswer: A root widening a rock crack

questions.question: What is erosion?
options: A rock changing in one place

questions.question: Which change is deposition?
options: Wind lifting grains off a dune

questions.question: To test slope, what should stay alike?
options: The height of both tray ends

questions.question: What is a limit of a soil-tray model?
options: It proves every hill acts alike
It leaves out parts of real hills
It must have no water in it
questions.correctAnswer: It leaves out parts of real hills

questions.question: Explain how a grain can experience erosion and deposition.
questions.expectedAnswer: Water can carry the grain away from one place, which is erosion, then leave it in a slower part of the stream, which is deposition.

questions.question: Why is water color not an exact soil-mass measurement?
questions.expectedAnswer: Color can depend on particle type, size, lighting, and concentration. A darker cup alone does not provide a measured mass of moved sediment.

data.question: Does erosion always happen slowly?
data.answer: No. A storm or slide can move a lot at once. Small changes can also build over time.

data.question: Is weathering the same as weather?
data.answer: No. Weather is the state of the air. Weathering is rock breaking down or changing in place.

data.question: Can plants change erosion?
data.answer: Yes. Roots and plant cover can hold soil and change water flow. Their effect depends on the setup.

data.question: Does all sediment settle at once?
data.answer: No. Grain size and water movement affect when and where material settles.
